text: According to a new report by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), international organized crime continues to pose a significant threat to global security, economy, and society. The study highlights the increasing sophistication and diversification of criminal networks, which are now involved in a wide range of activities, from drug trafficking and human smuggling to cybercrime and money laundering. The report also reveals that organized crime groups are becoming more transnational, with many operating in multiple countries and regions. The UNODC calls for greater international cooperation and coordination to combat this growing threat, as well as measures to address the root causes of criminality, such as poverty, inequality, and corruption.

Passage: Researchers have discovered that some individuals who have previously contracted polio may be at risk of developing a debilitating condition known as post-polio syndrome. The syndrome, which affects up to 30% of polio survivors, causes fatigue, weakness, and muscle wasting. The study, published in the journal Brain, found that the symptoms of post-polio syndrome are linked to changes in the brain's white matter, which is responsible for transmitting signals between different regions. The findings suggest that early diagnosis and treatment of post-polio syndrome may help to mitigate its effects on affected individuals.

The Hubble Space Telescope, now in its 30th year of operation, has made groundbreaking discoveries that have transformed our understanding of the universe. Some of its most significant achievements include capturing the first-ever image of a distant supernova, revealing the age of the universe to be around 13.7 billion years, and providing evidence for the existence of dark energy. Hubble has also helped us better understand the formation and evolution of galaxies, including the Milky Way, and has identified thousands of new exoplanets. Its high-resolution images have captivated the public and inspired a new generation of scientists, making it one of the most successful and influential scientific instruments in history.

New efforts are underway to protect several endangered species of mammals around the world. In Africa, conservationists are working to save the critically endangered mountain gorilla population, which has dwindled to just over 1,000 individuals. In Asia, the Chinese giant panda and the Sumatran orangutan are both facing threats from habitat loss and poaching, with less than 2,000 of each remaining in the wild. Meanwhile, in South America, the Brazilian authorities are cracking down on the trade of jaguar pelts and bones, which has contributed to a decline in the jaguar population. These and other endangered mammals are the focus of international conservation efforts, as scientists and activists work to ensure their survival for future generations.

Local authorities are warning drivers to be extra cautious on the roads as a spike in accidents involving dangerous vehicles has been reported. Police have received several complaints about cars and trucks with faulty brakes, worn-out tires, and malfunctioning lights. In response, law enforcement agencies are conducting rigorous inspections of vehicles and imposing strict penalties on drivers who fail to maintain their cars in good condition. The public is advised to avoid sharing the road with suspicious-looking vehicles and to report any unsafe vehicles to the authorities immediately.

At least 19 African civilians have been killed in airstrikes carried out by U.S. Forces in Somalia this week, according to reports by local officials and monitoring groups. The strikes targeted Al-Shabaab militants, who are linked to Al-Qaeda, but also resulted in civilian casualties, including women and children. The U.S. Military has not yet confirmed the number of casualties, but has stated that it takes all allegations of civilian harm seriously and conducts thorough investigations into such incidents. The U.S. Has increased its military operations against Al-Shabaab in recent years, with over 50 strikes reported in Somalia in 2020 alone.

In a recent development, several new hydroelectric projects have been announced in different parts of the world. In South America, Brazil's state-owned utility company, Eletrobras, has approved the construction of two new hydroelectric plants on the Teles Pires River in the Amazon region. The projects, with a combined capacity of 1,230 megawatts, are expected to provide clean energy to over 3 million people. In Asia, the Chinese government has given the green light to two new hydroelectric projects on the Mekong River, one in Laos and the other in Cambodia. These projects, with a total capacity of 1,380 megawatts, will generate electricity for both domestic use and export to neighboring countries. Advancements in dental technology have led to the rise of implant dentistry, a procedure that replaces missing teeth with artificial ones. Implant dentistry involves placing a small titanium screw into the jawbone, which acts as a root for the new tooth. This procedure offers several benefits, including improved chewing and speaking abilities, as well as a more natural-looking smile. With a success rate of over 95%, implant dentistry has become a popular and effective solution for those missing one or more teeth.

Rapper T.I. Was arrested on Wednesday morning in Georgia for simple assault, disorderly conduct, and public drunkenness. The incident occurred outside of a gated community where T.I. Resides, and involved a security guard who reportedly refused to let the rapper's friend enter the property. T.I. Allegedly came to the scene and got into a confrontation with the guard, leading to his arrest. This is not the first time T.I. Has run into legal trouble, as he served time in federal prison in 2009 for probation violations.

Scientists at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have discovered a new way to destroy brain cancer cells using radio waves. The study, published in the journal Science Translational Medicine, found that applying radio waves to tumors caused them to heat up and die, while leaving healthy cells unharmed. This non-invasive technique, called radiofrequency ablation, could potentially replace traditional surgery for certain types of brain cancer. The researchers are now working to refine the technology and test it in clinical trials.

In a recent development in the world of business, a major industrial espionage case has come to light. Authorities have accused a group of individuals working for a rival company of stealing sensitive intellectual property from their competitor. The stolen information reportedly includes trade secrets, product designs, and strategic plans, which could give the perpetrators a significant advantage in the market. The case has highlighted the growing concern over industrial espionage and the need for companies to take adequate measures to protect their valuable assets. The investigation is ongoing, and the perpetrators could face serious legal consequences if found guilty.

Hydroponics, the innovative farming technique that allows plants to grow without soil, is gaining popularity as a sustainable and efficient way to produce crops. This method involves suspending plant roots in nutrient-rich water, eliminating the need for traditional soil-based farming practices. Hydroponic systems can be operated indoors, using less water and space than traditional farming methods, making them ideal for urban areas and areas with limited resources. Hydroponics has been shown to increase crop yields and reduce the use of pesticides and fertilizers, making it an attractive option for environmentally conscious consumers. As the demand for fresh produce continues to rise, hydroponics is poised to revolutionize the way we grow and distribute food.

Magnetic levitation, or maglev for short, is a revolutionary transportation technology that uses powerful magnets to propel trains at high speeds without physical contact with the track. The first commercial maglev line opened in Shanghai, China, in 2004, and since then, the technology has gained widespread attention for its potential to revolutionize the way we travel. Maglev trains can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, making them significantly faster than traditional trains. The lack of friction between the train and the track also makes maglev trains more energy-efficient, as they require less power to operate. As research and development in maglev technology continue, it is likely that we will see more maglev lines popping up around the world, offering faster, more efficient, and more environmentally-friendly transportation options for commuters and travelers alike.

Scientists have discovered a new species of marine vegetation off the coast of Australia. Known as Halimeda rubiformis, this algae is distinguished by its bright red color and unique shape. The finding is significant as it adds to the growing understanding of the diverse marine life in the region and could have implications for the study of marine ecosystems and climate change. The new species has been documented in shallow waters near the Great Barrier Reef and is believed to play a crucial role in the local food chain. Further research is needed to determine the full extent of its ecological significance.

Authorities are investigating a series of unexplained highway accidents that have left several drivers injured in the past week. The incidents, which have occurred on different stretches of highway in the state, have left law enforcement officials baffled as there have been no obvious causes or signs of foul play. Witnesses have reported seeing strange lights and objects near the scenes of the accidents, but these claims have not been substantiated. As the investigation continues, authorities are urging drivers to exercise caution on the roads and report any suspicious activity to the police.

Polygamy, a social and cultural practice in which an individual is married to multiple spouses at the same time, can take on different forms. Polyandry, a less common variant, refers to a situation in which a woman is married to multiple men simultaneously. In contrast, polygyny is the practice of one man having multiple wives at the same time. While polygamy is still prevalent in some cultures and religions, it is also subject to legal and social restrictions in many parts of the world. The practice has sparked debates over issues such as gender equality, human rights, and religious freedom.

New federal rules aimed at combating the nuisance of unsolicited faxes go into effect on October 16. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, businesses will now require express written consent from individuals or companies before sending them fax advertisements. Failure to obtain consent could result in fines of up to $1,500 per violation. The new rules also require faxes to include opt-out instructions and contact information for the sender. The Federal Communications Commission estimates that the new rules will save American businesses and consumers billions of dollars annually.

As more and more baby boomers reach retirement age, the search for the best place to spend their golden years is on the rise. After careful consideration of various factors such as cost of living, healthcare, climate, and quality of life, several countries have emerged as top contenders. 

According to a recent report by International Living, Panama has claimed the top spot as the best retirement destination for 2021. With its tropical climate, affordable cost of living, and world-class healthcare system, Panama offers retirees a comfortable and relaxing lifestyle. 

Other countries making the list include Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador, and Portugal. Each of these destinations offers its unique charm and benefits, ranging from stunning natural scenery to a rich cultural heritage.

Scientists have made a breakthrough in the search for new fuel sources, announcing the discovery of a bacterium that can convert nitrite, a common air pollutant, into usable energy. This groundbreaking finding has the potential to revolutionize the way we produce and consume energy, as nitrite is widely available and could be harnessed as a sustainable alternative to traditional fossil fuels. The research team, led by Dr. Emma Stubbs at the University of Cambridge, has published their findings in the journal Nature Communications, and further studies are underway to explore the full potential of this exciting development.

Undersea fiber optic cables have revolutionized global communication by providing faster and more reliable data transmissions between continents. These cables, which are laid on the ocean floor, can stretch thousands of miles and carry vast amounts of information at lightning speed. The latest technology in fiber optics allows for higher bandwidth and lower latency, making these cables essential for modern-day connectivity. Recently, a new undersea cable called the Pacific Light Cable Network was activated, connecting Los Angeles and Hong Kong, further enhancing the connectivity between Asia and the Americas.

Women are making significant strides in politics around the world, with several countries breaking records for the number of female lawmakers in their parliaments. In Rwanda, women hold a record-breaking 61.3% of seats in the lower house of parliament, making it the most gender-balanced national legislature in the world. In neighboring Tanzania, women now hold 40.5% of seats in parliament, a significant increase from just 13% in 2005. In Argentina, women also recently made history by electing a female president, and now hold over 40% of seats in both the lower and upper houses of parliament. These achievements are a testament to the progress being made towards gender equality in politics, and a sign that more women will continue to be elected to office in the future.

In a shocking development in the world of art, authorities in Italy have announced the arrest of a notorious art thief accused of stealing several priceless works from museums and galleries across Europe. The suspect, identified as a 42-year-old Dutch national, has been on the run for over a decade and is believed to have amassed a fortune in stolen art, much of which remains missing. The investigation, which has spanned several countries, has been described as one of the largest and most complex art crime cases in recent history. The stolen artworks, which include paintings by renowned artists such as Picasso and Monet, are estimated to be worth millions of dollars. The case has highlighted the growing issue of international art crime and the need for increased cooperation between law enforcement agencies to combat this dangerous and lucrative criminal enterprise.

A prominent literary journal has come under fire for accusations of plagiarism in its latest issue. Several authors have spoken out, claiming that passages in their published pieces have been lifted without proper attribution or consent. The journal's editor has issued a statement acknowledging the errors and vowing to take swift action to rectify the situation. The incident has sparked a wider discussion in the literary community about the importance of originality and the need for rigorous fact-checking and plagiarism checks in journalistic and literary works.

The ties between Argentina and Britain have strengthened in recent months, according to a joint statement released by the foreign ministers of both countries. The statement, which was issued after a virtual meeting between Argentine Foreign Minister Santiago Cafiero and his British counterpart Dominic Raab, highlighted the progress made in areas such as trade, regional security, and climate change. The two ministers also discussed the ongoing dispute over the Falkland Islands, with Raab reiterating Britain's commitment to the self-governing territory's sovereignty, and Cafiero calling for dialogue and respect for international law. The statement marked a positive development in relations between the two countries, which have been strained in the past over issues such as the Falklands War and the UK's support for Argentina's debt restructuring.

In a recent trend, more and more people are embracing cult-inspired lifestyles as a way to find meaning and purpose in their lives. From meditation and mindfulness practices to communal living and alternative forms of spirituality, these movements offer a sense of community and connection that is increasingly appealing in a disconnected world. While some may view these lifestyles as fringe or extreme, advocates argue that they provide a path to inner peace, self-discovery, and social change. As interest in these movements continues to grow, experts warn of the potential risks and dangers of cult-like behavior, including brainwashing, manipulation, and exploitation. It remains to be seen whether these lifestyles will continue to gain mainstream acceptance or remain on the fringes of society.

In a tragic series of events, two ferries have sunk in separate incidents this week, claiming the lives of dozens of passengers. The first ferry, carrying over 100 people, sank off the coast of Indonesia on Tuesday, leaving at least 170 dead and dozens still missing. The cause of the sinking is still being investigated, but poor weather conditions are suspected. In a separate incident, a ferry capsized in Lake Victoria, Tanzania, on Thursday, killing at least 22 people. The overcrowded vessel was reportedly carrying more than twice its capacity when it overturned, leaving many passengers trapped inside. The incidents have highlighted the ongoing safety concerns on ferry services in some parts of the world, prompting calls for improved safety measures and regulation.

According to the latest Global Slavery Index, an estimated 40.3 million people are living in modern slavery worldwide. The report, released by the Walk Free Foundation, reveals that the majority of these individuals are trapped in forced labor, with debt bondage being the most prevalent form. The index also highlights that women and girls are disproportionately affected by modern slavery, making up 99% of victims in the commercial sex industry. The report calls for urgent action from governments, businesses, and civil society to end this heinous human rights violation.

Pope Francis has announced that he will beatify four individuals next month, including Spanish priest Gabriel García Moreno and Italian nun Laura Montoya Rey, during his trip to Ecuador. The beatification process is the final step before sainthood, and involves recognizing a person's life of heroic virtue and a proven miracle. García Moreno served as Ecuador's president and bishop in the late 19th century, while Montoya Rey founded the Sisters of the Holy Family in Colombia in the early 20th century. The other two individuals to be beatified are French priest Emmanuel Lévázy and Italian layman Giovanni Battista Scalabrini.

Mexico City, the capital of Mexico, continues to grapple with high levels of air pollution. According to recent data, the city's air quality index (AQI) has exceeded healthy limits, with fine particulate matter (PM2.5) reaching dangerous levels. The smog, which is a result of a combination of vehicular emissions, industrial activity, and natural sources, has triggered health warnings for vulnerable populations such as children, the elderly, and individuals with respiratory issues. The government has implemented measures to curb pollution, including limiting vehicle use on certain days and promoting public transportation and cycling. However, experts warn that more needs to be done to tackle the root causes of air pollution in Mexico City and other urban areas across the country.

Iran and Iraq have announced plans to strengthen their bilateral cooperation in various fields, including trade, agriculture, and energy. During a recent meeting between Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi and his Iraqi counterpart, Barham Salih, in Tehran, the two leaders stressed the importance of enhancing economic ties between the neighboring countries. They also discussed ways to increase Iran's exports of goods such as steel, cement, and petrochemicals to Iraq, as well as Iraq's imports of electricity from Iran. The leaders further emphasized the need to enhance security cooperation and combat common threats such as terrorism and organized crime. The move towards deeper cooperation between Iran and Iraq comes at a time when both countries are facing economic challenges and seek to mitigate the impact of US sanctions.

Amidst growing criticism from civil society groups and some developing countries, the World Bank has come under fire for its lending practices and alleged failure to prioritize poverty reduction. Critics argue that the Bank's focus on market-oriented solutions and structural adjustment programs has led to increased inequality and marginalization of vulnerable populations. They also accuse the Bank of promoting private sector interests over the needs of poor communities, and of failing to adequately consult with affected communities before implementing projects. The Bank has defended its approach, stating that it remains committed to reducing poverty and promoting sustainable development, but acknowledges the need for greater transparency and accountability. The Bank's President, David Malpass, has promised to engage in a "listening exercise" with stakeholders to better understand their concerns and address them.

The Indian government has launched a crackdown on income tax evasion, with authorities conducting raids and searches on several individuals and businesses suspected of concealing their income. The move is part of a larger effort to boost tax revenues and curb tax evasion, which is estimated to be a significant drain on the country's economy. The government has set a target of collecting over Rs 12 lakh crore ($16.5 billion) in direct taxes for the current financial year, and the drive against tax evasion is expected to help meet this goal. The authorities have also warned taxpayers to come clean and declare their income to avoid facing penalties and prosecution.

Amid growing concerns over antibiotic resistance, a team of scientists has discovered a new type of bacteria that has the ability to produce its own antibiotics. The findings, published in the journal Nature Microbiology, could lead to the development of new treatments for antibiotic-resistant diseases. The bacterium, named Streptomyces sp. Strain TI6-2, was isolated from soil in Thailand and was found to produce a previously unknown class of antibiotics called the Tiancins. The study highlights the importance of continuing research into the natural world for the discovery of new antibiotics and potential treatments for bacterial diseases.

The U.S. Government has tightened export controls on certain types of cryptography software and hardware, citing national security concerns. The new rules, which went into effect on October 15, require a license for the export of items that use specific quantum computing algorithms or have the ability to generate encryption keys. The restrictions are intended to prevent the spread of technologies that could potentially be used to break U.S. Encryption standards or disrupt critical infrastructure. The move is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to strengthen export controls across a range of emerging technologies.

A California couple has been granted the rights to raise a baby as both adoptive and biological parents. The couple, identified only as Rebecca and Matthew, underwent a groundbreaking fertility treatment that involved Rebecca carrying Matthew's embryo using a uterus donated by a relative. The procedure, known as "three-person IVF," allows couples with infertility issues to conceive a genetically related child using the mother's egg and father's sperm, but with a donated uterus. The baby, born in April, is the first in the U.S. To be conceived and born using the experimental technique. The couple's attorney called the decision by the San Mateo County Superior Court "a first-of-its-kind legal victory" and said it would allow other families to legally recognize both the genetic and gestational parents. In a shocking incident, a black bear attacked a group of hikers in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park in Tennessee on Sunday. According to park officials, the bear charged at the group of six hikers, injuring three of them before it was driven away by park rangers. The injured hikers, who have been identified as a 65-year-old woman, a 35-year-old man, and a 13-year-old boy, have been taken to the hospital for treatment. The park authorities have warned hikers to carry bear spray and make noise to avoid surprise attacks by the animals. The park remains open, but visitors have been advised to be cautious and aware of their surroundings. This is the second bear attack in the park this year, and the authorities have urged people to respect the wildlife and give them enough space.

According to recent data from the World Health Organization, viral hepatitis continues to be a major global health issue. An estimated 292 million people are currently living with chronic hepatitis B or C, with over 1.3 million deaths attributed to viral hepatitis each year. The WHO has set a goal to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health problem by 2030 and to reduce new hepatitis C infections by 80% by 2030. To achieve these targets, increased access to vaccination, testing, and treatment is needed, as well as efforts to address the social and economic factors that contribute to the spread of these diseases.

New research has shed light on the potential risks associated with long-term aspirin use, particularly for individuals who do not have a history of heart disease or stroke. The study, published in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, found that while aspirin can help prevent cardiovascular events in people with existing heart problems, it may also increase the risk of bleeding in the brain and stomach for those without such conditions. The findings suggest that doctors should carefully consider the benefits and risks of aspirin therapy on an individual basis, taking into account factors such as age, overall health, and personal risk of cardiovascular events.

Researchers at the University of Southern California have made a breakthrough in the development of a new drug to treat Alzheimer's disease. The drug, called USC2628, has shown promising results in animal trials, improving memory and cognitive function in mice with Alzheimer's-like symptoms. The drug targets a specific protein, called tau, which is believed to play a key role in the development of Alzheimer's. The study's findings, published in the journal ACS Chemical Neuroscience, offer hope for the future of Alzheimer's treatment and highlight the importance of continued research in this area. Clinical trials for the drug are expected to begin in the near future.

The international community has made significant progress in banning the use of landmines, with 164 countries having ratified the Mine Ban Treaty as of August 2021. The treaty, also known as the Ottawa Treaty, was adopted in 1997 and aims to eliminate stockpiles of antipersonnel mines and prevent their use in armed conflicts. Notably, the treaty has saved countless lives and prevented thousands of injuries, as landmines continue to pose a serious threat to civilians long after conflicts have ended. However, some countries, including Myanmar, Syria, and South Sudan, have yet to join the treaty, leaving millions of people in affected areas at risk of harm. Nonetheless, the global movement to ban landmines continues to gain momentum, with advocates calling for increased support and resources to help affected communities and ensure full implementation of the treaty.

As air travel continues to increase in popularity, airport security measures have become a top priority for aviation authorities around the world. In response to heightened security concerns, airports are implementing stricter screening procedures and investing in state-of-the-art technology to detect potential threats. These measures include advanced imaging systems, biometric identification methods, and increased staffing to ensure a more secure and efficient passenger experience. As the threat of terrorism and other security risks persists, airports are committed to staying ahead of the curve in their efforts to provide safe and secure air travel for all.

The United States has announced the expulsion of 60 Russian diplomats in response to the Kremlin's alleged involvement in a major cyber attack on a Swiss laboratory hosting a global chemical weapons watchdog. The move, described as a "diplomatic expulsion," follows a warning from the White House that President Biden would respond to any further Russian aggression with "a response in kind." The Swiss government has also confirmed the expulsion of four Russian officials in solidarity with the US action. The Russian embassy in Washington has condemned the decision, calling it "short-sighted and destructive."

In a tragic turn of events, four police officers lost their lives in the line of duty over the weekend. Two officers were shot and killed in separate incidents in Florida and California, while a third officer died after being struck by a vehicle in Texas. The fourth officer passed away following a battle with COVID-19. The fallen officers will be remembered and honored for their service and sacrifice to their communities. Their families and departments are mourning their loss and asking for continued support and respect for the men and women in blue.

Cybersecurity experts are warning of a surge in email scams, with a new report revealing a 600% increase in phishing attacks in the first quarter of 2021. These scams, known as phishing, use deceptive emails or messages to trick users into revealing sensitive information or downloading malware. The rise in these abuses of email, or e mails, is attributed to the ongoing pandemic and the shift to remote work, as cybercriminals take advantage of the increased reliance on digital communication. Users are urged to be vigilant and verify the authenticity of emails before taking any action.

According to the latest figures released by the Tobacco Institute of Eastern Europe (TIZE), the region's tobacco exports to overseas markets reached an all-time high in 2020, despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic. TIZE reports that tobacco sales to countries such as Germany, the UK, and the Netherlands increased by over 10% last year, with a total value of $1.2 billion. The organization attributes this growth to a rise in demand for high-quality tobacco and a shift towards alternative tobacco products, such as heated tobacco and snus, in response to stricter smoking bans. TIZE predicts that the trend towards increased tobacco exports will continue in 2021, as more consumers seek out premium tobacco products from Eastern Europe.

New educational standards aimed at preparing students for college and careers are being implemented in schools across the country. Known as the Common Core State Standards, these guidelines focus on critical thinking, problem-solving, and analytical skills. The standards have been adopted by 46 states and the District of Columbia, with the goal of ensuring that all students graduate from high school with the knowledge and skills necessary to succeed in higher education and the workforce. Critics of the Common Core argue that the standards place too much emphasis on testing and take away from traditional teaching methods, but supporters maintain that they provide a more rigorous and relevant education for today's students.

According to a recent report by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the world is witnessing an alarming rate of wildlife extinction. The report reveals that more than 40,000 species are currently at risk of extinction, with many already gone forever. Habitat loss, climate change, and poaching are identified as the major causes of this devastating trend. The IUCN urges immediate action from governments, conservation organizations, and individuals to protect endangered species and their habitats before it's too late.

Agoraphobia, a type of anxiety disorder, is on the rise during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to mental health experts. With lockdowns, social distancing, and increased isolation, many individuals are experiencing heightened fears of public spaces, crowds, and unfamiliar environments. Symptoms of agoraphobia include panic attacks, intense anxiety, and avoidance behaviors that can significantly impact daily life. As the pandemic continues, it's essential to prioritize mental health and seek professional help if agoraphobia or other anxiety disorders become a concern.

Scientists have made a groundbreaking discovery in the field of metabolism research. A team of researchers at the University of California, San Diego has identified a new pathway in the liver that regulates the breakdown of fats. The study, published in the journal Nature Communications, could have significant implications for the treatment of metabolic disorders such as obesity and diabetes. The findings suggest that targeting this pathway could help to reduce the accumulation of fat in the liver and improve overall metabolic health. Further research is needed to fully understand the potential therapeutic applications of this discovery.

Healthcare facilities across the country are implementing health computer terminals to improve patient care and streamline administrative tasks. These devices allow doctors and nurses to quickly access medical records, order tests, and communicate with specialists. Patients can also use them to check their own health information, schedule appointments, and communicate with their healthcare providers. The adoption of health computer terminals is expected to reduce wait times, improve accuracy, and ultimately lead to better health outcomes for patients.
